lines.text: Why does AI forget what you told it earlier?
It's called context rot.
The more its context holds, the worse it uses any one detail.
Nothing's deleted. It just slowly loses track.
You tell it your budget: five hundred dollars.
Two hundred messages later, it suggests a nine hundred dollar hotel.
Or in code: don't touch the migrations folder. Hours of logs later, it edits a migration.
So why does it happen? Step one.
Each token looks back at every token before it.
Four tokens make six links. A million make five hundred billion.
Step two. Each token has a fixed amount of attention to share.
More tokens, thinner slices.
And it was trained mostly on shorter texts.
Step three. Researchers found AI often uses the start and end best.
Stuff in the middle is the easiest to miss.
Step four. Look-alikes compete.
Your budget and your sister's. The old version of a file and the new one.
The more look-alikes, the more mix-ups.
So how do you fight it?
New topic? New chat.
Long chat? Get a summary and start fresh.
Repeat the facts that matter.
And give it only what it needs.
Context rot is real, but a tidy desk keeps it in check.
